title: Dhul Qa'dah

cards: A suitcase lies open on a bed, half full. Two lengths of plain white cloth, folded. A small bottle of unscented soap.
A list on the fridge of people to call before leaving: an aunt, an old friend, a neighbor they once argued with. Someone in this house is going on hajj.
The calendar has turned to Dhul Qa'dah, one of the sacred months from earlier on the path. Nothing big happens in it on the calendar. But in houses like this one, bags are being packed.

teach.b: First, it sits inside the season of the pilgrimage. Surah al-Baqarah says, in Pickthall's translation: "The pilgrimage is (in) the well-known months."
Tradition counts Dhul Qa'dah among them, so travelers can already be on the road. Second, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose this month for his own journeys to Makkah.
Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet's 'umrahs, the lesser pilgrimages, were in Dhul Qa'dah, except the one he joined to his hajj. Third, packing.
The same verse goes on: "So make provision for yourselves (Hereafter); for the best provision is to ward off evil." Pack your bag, it says, and then it names a provision no bag can hold.
So for some pilgrims, getting ready means paying back what they owe and asking forgiveness from people they've wronged: the calls on the fridge list. Fourth, the people who stay.

In al-Tirmidhi, when someone was leaving, the Prophet would say, in paraphrase: I entrust to Allah your religion, what you've been trusted with, and the last of your deeds. Not a wish for good weather.

how: In Dhul Qa'dah, Muslims preparing for hajj often settle debts, ask forgiveness of family and friends, and gather their simple white garments, and families and mosques send them off with prayers for a safe journey.

o: the sacred month just before the hajj
the month when Ramadan's fast is kept
the white cloth pilgrims wear on hajj

p: the Prophet's words to a traveler

s: the Qur'an tells pilgrims to bring no provisions
it says "make provision for yourselves," then names the best provision: to ward off evil.
Anas reports the Prophet's 'umrahs were in Dhul Qa'dah, except the one joined to his hajj
the month already had his footsteps in it.
Dhul Qa'dah is one of the sacred months
it's the first of the three that come one after another.

games.q: you're packing for the pilgrimage. the verse says make provision for yourselves. what does it call the best provision?
games.why: "for the best provision is to ward off evil." the verse starts with packing and ends with something no bag can hold.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is going on hajj, or has gone, or hopes to go someday; if no one comes, picture a stranger in white at an airport gate, a little nervous, passport in hand.
Stay with their packing and their goodbyes for a few breaths. If you pray, use the Prophet's farewell, I entrust you to Allah; if not, wish them a safe road and a good return.

wordCard.voice: Dhul Qa'dah. A sacred month, the month before the hajj, when the Prophet made his 'umrahs and when pilgrims pack, settle their debts and say their goodbyes. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of a sacred month, the first of the three that come one after another.

carryVoice: Your line: the pilgrims set out. And the ones at home hand them over. Tomorrow, Dhul Hijjah at home.

sources.q: The pilgrimage is (in) the well-known months
So make provision for yourselves (Hereafter); for the best provision is to ward off evil.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1778 (Anas: the Prophet's 'umrahs in Dhul Qa'dah, except the one with his hajj)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4662 (Abu Bakrah: the farewell sermon names the sacred months, three in a row beginning with Dhul Qa'dah)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3443 (the farewell to a traveler: I entrust to Allah your religion, your trust, and the last of your deeds)
